# Steering-lite BS-bench rewrite

Continue the approved benchmark rewrite from vjp-steering on `rewrite/bsbench-vjp`. Finish the cheap first sycophancy comparison, preserve the completed local and fake-path work, and use the recovered pi-goals worker path after approval.

## User-visible result

A clean cached Modal `just sweep` compares steering-lite, VJP-cache and VJP-diff with bare, prompting, random, mean-difference and PCA controls on 20 numbered Qwen3.5-4B BS-bench v2 questions. It uses a cheap four-prompt dose calibration, tests method/model-specific RMS-KL transfer on four disjoint cases, and saves persona validation, aware and blind judgments, costs, reference-style HTML/PNG plots, and maximum-coherent/1:4-optimal tables for less than $50.

## Preferences and authority

- Initial Modal and judge work together must remain below $50. Use Terra or DeepSeek V4 Flash workers, not Astra, and keep one implementation writer.
- Preserve the existing aware judge protocol and separate blind call. Score every measured dose as directed intended effect − 4 × off-target effect and retain the full Pareto frontier.
- The score is a ranking statistic, not a pass threshold. The judge's off-axis value is an outcome, not a coherence threshold. Never suppress the main evaluation or RMS-KL transfer because a score is negative or an off-axis value exceeds an invented cutoff.
- Use the existing four-prompt candidate grid to choose each method's highest observed dose without generation-health failures. Measure its RMS-KL target, predict matching coefficients on the 20-question evaluation cohort and four disjoint transfer cases, then evaluate 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× predicted doses. Retain incoherent or poor-scoring outputs as measured failures.
- The 20-question evaluation answers which method is powerful and precise. Only the four disjoint cases test RMS-KL transfer. Do not describe the four-prompt calibration grid as the completed benchmark.
- After a successful settled probe, continue the approved eight-method sweep without another approval pause. Re-run a cache-aware dry budget check first.
- On a paid-stage failure, stop later dispatch, preserve and reconcile the ledger, fix and retry only the affected cached stage. Repeat the exact blocker in each user update until the user can fix it. Never substitute a model or fallback silently.
- If RMS-KL transfer is negative, rule out code and evaluation errors within the existing budget, then report the audited negative result without changing the metric or datasets after seeing results.
- This is experimental development, not publication proof. Do not post publicly or spend on larger models without separate approval.

## User voice

> can we add VJP-cache and VJP-diff

> yes please. also I wonder if we should uplift steering-lite to match vjp-steering so
>
> - **pairs** I would bring in minimal things in a clean way from  https://github.com/wassname/persona-steering-template-library, namely consider judge validation of the prefix and suffix? and perhaps it can be the same judge and reused from the eval? ok that's the steering personas
>   - but I would also like to use the judge (slow) or activation or J lens to validate if the person pairs correspond to the intended  
> - **calibration** I'm searching for a good way to calibrate so I can find the best dose cheaply and compare pareto optimal or max doses. A grid search is the most expensive. An iteratitive search such as an method of successive approximation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterative_method) is faster. But I'v found that (https://github.com/wassname/isokl_steering_calibration). I hope It can find the hyperparameter "target rmse(KL) [nats]" once per method/model, and it will allow quick calibration from then on. I would like to prove this... showing it predict's the max coherent dose on other datasets. (in any case it's better than what other papers and libraries do which is: no think about or talk about this at all, or do a super expensive grid search which I just can't afford).
> - **eval: faithfull** I found using a judge it usefull when the eval is not fully aligned with the steering, the judge can tell use "the effect is bluntness" but we aimed for honesty. another steering method might be more faithful. In fact the eval I used in jvp-steering seems good: it's fairly cheap (100 generations), fairly sensitive, has a nice graph showing the parto, and people understand sycophancy.
> - **platform** run on modal for speed, and still at low cost, and able to scale up from the initial Qwen 3.5 4B model to ~30B or 100+B
>
> so in the end I hope to redo steering-lite with a bullshit bench v2, judged eval, and my nice plot. Hopefully I can have a max dose and optimal dose table too. And compare to prompting as a baseline. Keeping the random zone, and mean mass diff, and PCA baseline.
>
> I migth use the 20 q dev versions first. ofc  the eval needs to be numbered. 
> In the end I hope to show the best steering method, ansering these questions
>
> which is the best (powerful and precise)?
> is it reliable? does it steer the concept we want fiathfully? does it scale to larger models? and I want a) html plot like vjp-steering (you need to view both png's and compare parity), b) corresponding max dose, and pareto optimal table
>

1. [/] goal: Run the real numbered BS-bench v2 comparison for VJP-cache, VJP-diff and all controls
   - scope: reuse vjp-steering; keep cache Gram; use bare, prompting, random, mean difference and PCA; VJP-diff is the existing VJP-delta method, not a duplicate.

   - discriminator: all eight conditions have numbered Qwen3.5-4B outputs on the 20-question evaluation cohort; each activation method has measured signed 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× predicted doses and complete judgments.
   - evidence: the pinned reference audit found that local runs used an invented judge model, replaced the second aware pass with blind calls, omitted `-C`, changed the reference layer/VJP configuration, and used one random seed rather than a random region. Existing one-sided activation results are superseded; paid work is paused.
2. [/] goal: Validate persona pairs and save judged effects plus blind change descriptions
   - subtle failure mode: style or metadata leakage substitutes for intended sycophancy movement, or a judge failure is treated as no change.
   - discriminator: saved bare/sycophantic/abrasive examples, full reference-aware AB/BA two-pass records plus separate target-blind records, numbered outputs and disagreements expose what changed and why.
   - evidence: the paired generations and local structural checks remain reusable. The 12 persona decisions and aware/blind records used `deepseek/deepseek-chat`, so they are historical evidence and must be rejudged with the pinned reference model and protocol.
3. [/] goal: Calibrate doses cheaply and test method/model-specific RMS-KL transfer on four disjoint cases
   - subtle failure mode: an invented behavioral cutoff blocks the experiment, calibration prompts masquerade as final evaluation, reused prompts masquerade as transfer, or one-sided calibration is called bidirectional steering.
   - discriminator: for each activation method, the highest candidate magnitude healthy in both directions defines one pooled signed RMS-KL target; saved iterative histories predict positive and negative coefficients on the evaluation cohort and four disjoint cases; signed 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× generations test those predictions and retain late failures.
   - evidence: the current candidate/final graph is one-sided and uses layer 3 rather than the reference-range full-attention subset. Corrected signed calibration, RMS-KL targets, predictions and generations have not run.
4. [/] goal: Complete the cached Modal `just sweep` below the initial $50 budget
   - subtle failure mode: cached calibration is mistaken for a complete sweep, an invalid old judgment is reused, a retry pays again, or conservative reserves are counted as invoices.
   - discriminator: a cache-aware preflight bounds only corrected missing work below $50; the corrected sweep completes goals 1–3; an unchanged rerun adds no GPU function call, provider request or ledger row.
   - evidence: ledger reconciliation and cache transport work. The old `$29.79` upper describes the wrong model/protocol and cannot authorize the corrected run; a new estimate is required after implementation.
5. [/] goal: Produce real reference-style HTML/PNG Pareto plots and maximum-coherent/optimal-dose tables
   - subtle failure mode: polished calibration-only or one-sided plots are labeled as the final comparison, a single random vector is called a random region, or poor and incoherent outputs are omitted.
   - discriminator: one measured-points artifact from the completed signed 20-question evaluation feeds both PNGs, HTML and tables; all evaluated doses remain visible; selected rows trace to numbered judgments and health records.
   - evidence: the renderer contract is reusable. Current plots and tables derive from the wrong judge protocol and one-sided generations, so they are superseded.

# Steering-lite BS-bench rewrite

Continue the approved benchmark rewrite from vjp-steering on `rewrite/bsbench-vjp`. Finish the cheap first sycophancy comparison, preserve the completed local and fake-path work, and use the recovered pi-goals worker path after approval.

## User-visible result

A clean cached Modal `just sweep` compares steering-lite, VJP-cache and VJP-diff with bare, prompting, random, mean-difference and PCA controls on 20 numbered Qwen3.5-4B BS-bench v2 questions. It uses a cheap four-prompt dose calibration, tests method/model-specific RMS-KL transfer on four disjoint cases, and saves persona validation, aware and blind judgments, costs, reference-style HTML/PNG plots, and maximum-coherent/1:4-optimal tables for less than $50.

## Preferences and authority

- Initial Modal and judge work together must remain below $50. Use Terra or DeepSeek V4 Flash workers, not Astra, and keep one implementation writer.
- Preserve the existing aware judge protocol and separate blind call. Score every measured dose as directed intended effect − 4 × off-target effect and retain the full Pareto frontier.
- The score is a ranking statistic, not a pass threshold. The judge's off-axis value is an outcome, not a coherence threshold. Never suppress the main evaluation or RMS-KL transfer because a score is negative or an off-axis value exceeds an invented cutoff.
- Use the existing four-prompt candidate grid to choose each method's highest observed dose without generation-health failures. Measure its RMS-KL target, predict matching coefficients on the 20-question evaluation cohort and four disjoint transfer cases, then evaluate 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× predicted doses. Retain incoherent or poor-scoring outputs as measured failures.
- The 20-question evaluation answers which method is powerful and precise. Only the four disjoint cases test RMS-KL transfer. Do not describe the four-prompt calibration grid as the completed benchmark.
- After a successful settled probe, continue the approved eight-method sweep without another approval pause. Re-run a cache-aware dry budget check first.
- On a paid-stage failure, stop later dispatch, preserve and reconcile the ledger, fix and retry only the affected cached stage. Repeat the exact blocker in each user update until the user can fix it. Never substitute a model or fallback silently.
- If RMS-KL transfer is negative, rule out code and evaluation errors within the existing budget, then report the audited negative result without changing the metric or datasets after seeing results.
- This is experimental development, not publication proof. Do not post publicly or spend on larger models without separate approval.

## User voice

> can we add VJP-cache and VJP-diff

> yes please. also I wonder if we should uplift steering-lite to match vjp-steering so
>
> - **pairs** I would bring in minimal things in a clean way from  https://github.com/wassname/persona-steering-template-library, namely consider judge validation of the prefix and suffix? and perhaps it can be the same judge and reused from the eval? ok that's the steering personas
>   - but I would also like to use the judge (slow) or activation or J lens to validate if the person pairs correspond to the intended  
> - **calibration** I'm searching for a good way to calibrate so I can find the best dose cheaply and compare pareto optimal or max doses. A grid search is the most expensive. An iteratitive search such as an method of successive approximation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterative_method) is faster. But I'v found that (https://github.com/wassname/isokl_steering_calibration). I hope It can find the hyperparameter "target rmse(KL) [nats]" once per method/model, and it will allow quick calibration from then on. I would like to prove this... showing it predict's the max coherent dose on other datasets. (in any case it's better than what other papers and libraries do which is: no think about or talk about this at all, or do a super expensive grid search which I just can't afford).
> - **eval: faithfull** I found using a judge it usefull when the eval is not fully aligned with the steering, the judge can tell use "the effect is bluntness" but we aimed for honesty. another steering method might be more faithful. In fact the eval I used in jvp-steering seems good: it's fairly cheap (100 generations), fairly sensitive, has a nice graph showing the parto, and people understand sycophancy.
> - **platform** run on modal for speed, and still at low cost, and able to scale up from the initial Qwen 3.5 4B model to ~30B or 100+B
>
> so in the end I hope to redo steering-lite with a bullshit bench v2, judged eval, and my nice plot. Hopefully I can have a max dose and optimal dose table too. And compare to prompting as a baseline. Keeping the random zone, and mean mass diff, and PCA baseline.

>
> the judge must also (this is a bew feature) 1) guess the concept being steered (ideally blind) this will tell us how faithfull it in
>

## Goals

1. [/] goal: Run the real numbered BS-bench v2 comparison for VJP-cache, VJP-diff and all controls
   - scope: reuse vjp-steering; keep cache Gram; use bare, prompting, random, mean difference and PCA; VJP-diff is the existing VJP-delta method, not a duplicate.
   - subtle failure mode: four calibration prompts or a cache-only rerun is reported as the requested comparison.
   - discriminator: all eight conditions have numbered Qwen3.5-4B outputs on the 20-question evaluation cohort; each activation method has measured 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× predicted doses and complete judgments.
   - evidence: extraction, attachment, Modal transport and candidate caches work; only bare and prompting currently have 20-question outputs. No activation method has final evaluation outputs.
2. [✓] goal: Validate persona pairs and save judged effects plus blind change descriptions
   - subtle failure mode: style or metadata leakage substitutes for intended sycophancy movement, or a judge failure is treated as no change.
   - discriminator: saved bare/sycophantic/abrasive examples, full aware AB/BA and target-blind request/response records, numbered outputs and disagreements expose what changed and why.
   - evidence: 12 real persona validations and complete aware/blind candidate records are saved; two persona disagreements remain visible. Final-evaluation judgments remain part of goals 1 and 3.
3. [/] goal: Calibrate doses cheaply and test method/model-specific RMS-KL transfer on four disjoint cases
   - subtle failure mode: an invented behavioral cutoff blocks the experiment, calibration prompts masquerade as final evaluation, or reused prompts masquerade as transfer.
   - discriminator: for each activation method, the highest candidate dose without generation-health failures defines an RMS-KL target; saved iterative histories predict coefficients on the evaluation cohort and four disjoint cases; 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× generations test those predictions and retain late failures.
   - evidence: candidate grids and judged calibration outputs exist; RMS-KL targets, search histories, transfer predictions and transfer generations have not run.
4. [/] goal: Complete the cached Modal `just sweep` below the initial $50 budget
   - subtle failure mode: cached calibration is mistaken for a complete sweep, a retry pays again, or conservative reserves are counted as invoices.
   - discriminator: a cache-aware preflight bounds only remaining work below $50; the corrected sweep completes goals 1 and 3; an unchanged rerun adds no GPU function call, provider request or ledger row.
   - evidence: cache transport and reconciliation work; conservative committed accounting is `$11.1300113737`, but the remaining corrected graph needs a new dry estimate.
5. [/] goal: Produce real reference-style HTML/PNG Pareto plots and maximum-coherent/optimal-dose tables
   - subtle failure mode: polished calibration-only plots are labeled as the final comparison or omit poor and incoherent final outputs.
   - discriminator: one measured-points artifact from the completed 20-question evaluation feeds both PNGs, HTML and tables; all evaluated doses remain visible; selected rows trace to numbered judgments and health records.
   - evidence: the renderer and visual review workflow work, but the current 44-point report contains calibration observations rather than final activation-method evaluation results.

## UAT / Verification

Open the real HTML report and both PNGs beside the vjp-steering references. Confirm that activation-method points come from the 20-question evaluation, not the four calibration prompts. Inspect selected and failing numbered answer pairs, blind descriptions, persona disagreements, RMS-KL search histories, four-case transfer results and ledger receipts. Rerun the same `just sweep` and verify no GPU function call, provider request or ledger row. Trace every plotted/table point to the saved measured-point and judgment records.

## Future work / out of scope

The 100-question evaluation and ~30B/100B models need separate spending approval. Do not claim publication-level or larger-model reliability. Do not add new concepts, trained objectives or an unrelated J-lens framework.

# Steering-lite BS-bench rewrite

Continue the approved benchmark rewrite from vjp-steering on `rewrite/bsbench-vjp`. Finish the cheap first sycophancy comparison, preserve the completed local and fake-path work, and use the recovered pi-goals worker path after approval.

## User-visible result

A clean cached Modal `just sweep` compares steering-lite, VJP-cache and VJP-diff with bare, prompting, random, mean-difference and PCA controls on 20 numbered Qwen3.5-4B BS-bench v2 questions. It uses a cheap four-prompt dose calibration, tests method/model-specific RMS-KL transfer on four disjoint cases, and saves persona validation, aware and blind judgments, costs, reference-style HTML/PNG plots, and maximum-coherent/1:4-optimal tables for less than $50.

## Preferences and authority

- Initial Modal and judge work together must remain below $50. Use Terra or DeepSeek V4 Flash workers, not Astra, and keep one implementation writer.
- Preserve the existing aware judge protocol and separate blind call. Score every measured dose as directed intended effect − 4 × off-target effect and retain the full Pareto frontier.
- The score is a ranking statistic, not a pass threshold. The judge's off-axis value is an outcome, not a coherence threshold. Never suppress the main evaluation or RMS-KL transfer because a score is negative or an off-axis value exceeds an invented cutoff.
- Use the existing four-prompt candidate grid to choose each method's highest observed dose without generation-health failures. Measure its RMS-KL target, predict matching coefficients on the 20-question evaluation cohort and four disjoint transfer cases, then evaluate 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× predicted doses. Retain incoherent or poor-scoring outputs as measured failures.
- The 20-question evaluation answers which method is powerful and precise. Only the four disjoint cases test RMS-KL transfer. Do not describe the four-prompt calibration grid as the completed benchmark.
- After a successful settled probe, continue the approved eight-method sweep without another approval pause. Re-run a cache-aware dry budget check first.
- On a paid-stage failure, stop later dispatch, preserve and reconcile the ledger, fix and retry only the affected cached stage. Repeat the exact blocker in each user update until the user can fix it. Never substitute a model or fallback silently.
- If RMS-KL transfer is negative, rule out code and evaluation errors within the existing budget, then report the audited negative result without changing the metric or datasets after seeing results.
- This is experimental development, not publication proof. Do not post publicly or spend on larger models without separate approval.

## User voice

>
> - **pairs** I would bring in minimal things in a clean way from  https://github.com/wassname/persona-steering-template-library, namely consider judge validation of the prefix and suffix? and perhaps it can be the same judge and reused from the eval? ok that's the steering personas
>   - but I would also like to use the judge (slow) or activation or J lens to validate if the person pairs correspond to the intended  
> - **calibration** I'm searching for a good way to calibrate so I can find the best dose cheaply and compare pareto optimal or max doses. A grid search is the most expensive. An iteratitive search such as an method of successive approximation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterative_method) is faster. But I'v found that (https://github.com/wassname/isokl_steering_calibration). I hope It can find the hyperparameter "target rmse(KL) [nats]" once per method/model, and it will allow quick calibration from then on. I would like to prove this... showing it predict's the max coherent dose on other datasets. (in any case it's better than what other papers and libraries do which is: no think about or talk about this at all, or do a super expensive grid search which I just can't afford).
> - **eval: faithfull** I found using a judge it usefull when the eval is not fully aligned with the steering, the judge can tell use "the effect is bluntness" but we aimed for honesty. another steering method might be more faithful. In fact the eval I used in jvp-steering seems good: it's fairly cheap (100 generations), fairly sensitive, has a nice graph showing the parto, and people understand sycophancy.

## Goals

1. [/] goal: Run the real numbered BS-bench v2 comparison for VJP-cache, VJP-diff and all controls
   - scope: reuse vjp-steering; keep cache Gram; use bare, prompting, random, mean difference and PCA; VJP-diff is the existing VJP-delta method, not a duplicate.
   - subtle failure mode: four calibration prompts or a cache-only rerun is reported as the requested comparison.
   - discriminator: all eight conditions have numbered Qwen3.5-4B outputs on the 20-question evaluation cohort; each activation method has measured 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× predicted doses and complete judgments.
   - evidence: extraction, attachment, Modal transport and candidate caches work; only bare and prompting currently have 20-question outputs. No activation method has final evaluation outputs.
2. [✓] goal: Validate persona pairs and save judged effects plus blind change descriptions
   - subtle failure mode: style or metadata leakage substitutes for intended sycophancy movement, or a judge failure is treated as no change.
   - discriminator: saved bare/sycophantic/abrasive examples, full aware AB/BA and target-blind request/response records, numbered outputs and disagreements expose what changed and why.
   - evidence: 12 real persona validations and complete aware/blind candidate records are saved; two persona disagreements remain visible. Final-evaluation judgments remain part of goals 1 and 3.
3. [/] goal: Calibrate doses cheaply and test method/model-specific RMS-KL transfer on four disjoint cases
   - subtle failure mode: an invented behavioral cutoff blocks the experiment, calibration prompts masquerade as final evaluation, or reused prompts masquerade as transfer.
   - discriminator: for each activation method, the highest candidate dose without generation-health failures defines an RMS-KL target; saved iterative histories predict coefficients on the evaluation cohort and four disjoint cases; 0.8×/1.0×/1.2× generations test those predictions and retain late failures.
   - evidence: candidate grids and judged calibration outputs exist; RMS-KL targets, search histories, transfer predictions and transfer generations have not run.
4. [/] goal: Complete the cached Modal `just sweep` below the initial $50 budget
   - subtle failure mode: cached calibration is mistaken for a complete sweep, a retry pays again, or conservative reserves are counted as invoices.
   - discriminator: a cache-aware preflight bounds only remaining work below $50; the corrected sweep completes goals 1 and 3; an unchanged rerun adds no GPU function call, provider request or ledger row.
   - evidence: cache transport and reconciliation work; conservative committed accounting is `$11.1300113737`, but the remaining corrected graph needs a new dry estimate.
5. [/] goal: Produce real reference-style HTML/PNG Pareto plots and maximum-coherent/optimal-dose tables
   - subtle failure mode: polished calibration-only plots are labeled as the final comparison or omit poor and incoherent final outputs.
   - discriminator: one measured-points artifact from the completed 20-question evaluation feeds both PNGs, HTML and tables; all evaluated doses remain visible; selected rows trace to numbered judgments and health records.
   - evidence: the renderer and visual review workflow work, but the current 44-point report contains calibration observations rather than final activation-method evaluation results.

## UAT / Verification

Open the real HTML report and both PNGs beside the vjp-steering references. Confirm that activation-method points come from the 20-question evaluation, not the four calibration prompts. Inspect selected and failing numbered answer pairs, blind descriptions, persona disagreements, RMS-KL search histories, four-case transfer results and ledger receipts. Rerun the same `just sweep` and verify no GPU function call, provider request or ledger row. Trace every plotted/table point to the saved measured-point and judgment records.

## Future work / out of scope

The 100-question evaluation and ~30B/100B models need separate spending approval. Do not claim publication-level or larger-model reliability. Do not add new concepts, trained objectives or an unrelated J-lens framework.

# Token-Efficient Logging for ML

Goal: let a context-poor agent see what ran, detect problems, and find the evidence needed to diagnose them without reading a noisy log.

## Two Markdown sinks

Write each message once. INFO goes to stdout and `run.md`; DEBUG goes only to `run.md`. Both are plain Markdown: no emojis, level icons, ANSI colors, or timestamp prefixes. The file is the live log with additional diagnostics, not a different report generated at the end. Open it before work starts and preserve it after failures. Fence tracebacks, config and raw text; leave blank lines around headings and tables. See the [minimal working example](references/python-logging.md).

Keep transient ASCII progress bars on stderr, outside both Markdown sinks. Raw JSONL, tensors and third-party output can remain separate linked artifacts. Do not strip Unicode from actual model outputs or data. -- Codex

## Always do

1. After attaching the logger, print `argv` and the pretty, resolved config actually used.
2. The log file is `run.md` and must be valid markdown, because it is also the result page: headings, tables, and links render, and one file per run means no second artifact to keep in sync. Head each stage with a Markdown heading and identifiers (`# train ...`), and each sub-stage with the breadcrumb path from its parent (`## train -> calibrating -> demo gen +ve (C=1.4)`). Separate with two newlines; close a stage with elapsed time and peak GPU memory when relevant.
3. Treat most diagnostic expectations as unvalidated. Start them with `TODO validate:`; use `FIXME:` for observed breakage. Reserve `SHOULD:` for a prediction backed by a mechanism, derivation, paper, or validated prior run. Keep the statement beside the evidence it interprets.
4. For every LLM-facing stage, save one full real demo produced through the normal code path: context, prompt, reply, and all special tokens. Do this for the first train/chosen/rejected, calibration, evaluation, and generation sample that exists.
5. Keep stdout sparse. Send extra Markdown diagnostics through DEBUG to the same file sink. Link bulky raw artifacts. Use ASCII tqdm on stderr with both `mininterval=120` and `maxinterval=120`; do not print every step.
6. After timing, cleanup and all other output, emit the headline metric, full copyable result table and run identity. The last nonblank line is the project-relative path to `run.md`. Inspect the actual final 40 lines, not an earlier result call. On failure, show the failed stage/error and link its full traceback; preserve the nonzero exit status.
7. The same key result table reaches stdout and `run.md`, laid out by the `markdown-tables` skill. Measured diagnostics belong in the DEBUG sink; speculative interpretation and research decisions belong in the task spec or journal via `arj`. Lead with task behavior or the completed functional smoke, not test counts. The curated cross-run `docs/results.md` is `setup-repo` 6b.
8. Disclosure by surface. The append-only JSONL / Inspect `.eval` is the single source of truth: every prompt, special token, separator, reasoning/thinking block, both judge orders, usage, and errors, verbatim. Every other surface is a compressed VIEW of it for a different reader. Two invariants hold on ALL surfaces: (a) always print a relative-from-project-root link to the source, ideally `path:line`, so the reader can drop to full fidelity; (b) never paraphrase in a way that changes meaning or silently omits a failure mode (mislabelled, incoherent, truncated, refusing, saturated, confounded). The reason is the ml-debug "look at the data / inspect the data first" check: the reader catches bad data only from the raw, so a digest without a link disables their main debugging tool. What varies per surface is only how much you compress:

   | surface | reader | compression | must include |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | JSONL / `.eval` | source of truth | none, everything verbatim | it IS the source |
   | `run.md` / stdout | agent or human scanning "what ran, what is the result, where is the evidence" | summarise (full traces every line would litter it); one full demo per LLM stage, see item 4; the result table in full, see item 7 | log path + `jsonl:line` |
   | chat (right now) | human doing "look at the data" | FULL verbatim when they say "show / display / paste / let me see"; formatting may HIGHLIGHT or REORGANISE (bold the diff, table, sections) but never drop, elide with "...", or paraphrase; show ALL variants, not one | inline full + jsonl link |
   | paper / blog | skeptical outsider | curated for narrative, but the shown trace is a real verbatim excerpt with the minimal diff highlighted | no paraphrase-as-quote, no hidden confounder, cite the trace |

   Byte-identical blocks across variants may be shown once, but say so explicitly. All of these are defaults the user can override either way ("just summarise" / "show me everything inline"). "Show me" means reproduce, not describe.

## Compose Markdown sections

Use one triple-quoted f-string for a coherent Markdown section. Compute variable blocks first, then interpolate them; do not emit one call per blank line or invent a Markdown wrapper just to remove indentation.

```python
table = tabulate(rows, headers=headers, tablefmt="pipe", disable_numparse=True)
log(f"""\\
## evaluation

{table}
""")
```

Use `tabulate` when it is already a project dependency and the table comes from an iterable of rows. Do not add it solely to print a static streaming header; keep that header as Markdown and append the data rows as they are measured. Jinja is for a maintained page template with repeated layout, not a single log section.

## Read only when needed

- When configuring Python sinks, progress bars, resolved config, or stage boundaries, read [references/python-logging.md](references/python-logging.md).
- When writing or auditing `TODO validate:`, `FIXME:`, or `SHOULD:` diagnostics, read [references/diagnostic-statements.md](references/diagnostic-statements.md).
- When logging prompts, chosen/rejected examples, calibration, evaluation, generations, or safety-task text, read [references/llm-traces.md](references/llm-traces.md).
- When formatting the final 40 lines, sweep summaries, or streaming per-step tables, read [references/results-and-tables.md](references/results-and-tables.md).
</skill>

# Markdown results tables

## The rule

It is a publication table. Ink and leftmost above-the-fold space are the two scarce resources, so
spend both only on what answers the reader's question. Order left to right by decreasing
importance and top to bottom by rank. Make typography carry meaning rather than decoration.

Everything below follows from that. Remember the rule and you will get most of it right.

## Consequences

1. Column 1 is the index, linked to its source. Then short metadata if rows need it. Then the
   headline score. Nothing else goes left of the headline.
2. The headline's own inputs follow it, in formula order, so the arithmetic is checkable in place.
3. Sort by the headline, best first. The answer is the first line read.
4. A unicode arrow on every header, glued to the last word: `sel↑`, `off↓`, `drift→0`. A space
   there lets the header wrap and strand the arrow on its own line, which was visible in both VS
   Code previews.
5. Bold the best cell per column, unless the best value covers over half the column. Seven bold
   `1.00`s out of thirteen rows say nothing. Italicise controls and baselines.
6. Always carry the floors and the bar. A number with nothing to beat means nothing.
7. Short headers. A header sets its column's width for every row below it. Definitions live in
   the caption.
8. One table per comparable group, most recent on top, identical columns in each.
9. Last column `notes` is free real estate: links to the evidence, and `<!-- CLAUDE: ... -->`
   comments that are invisible rendered but readable by the next agent.

## Example, before and after

wassname's, from dqre. Already good: name links to `file#line` so provenance costs no width, then
metadata, then the headline `F2`, then the components `F2` is made of, sorted by headline.

```markdown
| subspace | form | F2 | recall: en at L27 | leak: fr at L32 | precision |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [`en_minus_null`](dqre/subspaces.py#L176) | shared | 0.37 | 0.33 | +0.16 | 0.68 |
| [`unembed_top`](dqre/subspaces.py#L119) | shared | 0.21 | 0.17 | +0.07 | 0.71 |
| [`en_minus_null_perp_all`](dqre/subspaces.py#L180) | shared | 0.19 | 0.16 | +0.05 | 0.76 |
```

Missing arrows, bold-best, a floor, and the headers are long. Fixed:

```markdown
| subspace | form | F2 ↑ | recall en@L27 ↑ | leak fr@L32 ↓ | precision ↑ | notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| [`en_minus_null`](dqre/subspaces.py#L176) | shared | **0.37** | **+0.33** | +0.16 | 0.68 | [res](out/a.jsonl) |
| [`unembed_top`](dqre/subspaces.py#L119) | shared | 0.21 | +0.17 | +0.07 | 0.71 | [res](out/b.jsonl) |
| [`en_minus_null_perp_all`](dqre/subspaces.py#L180) | shared | 0.19 | +0.16 | **+0.05** | **0.76** | [res](out/c.jsonl) |
| *[`random_rank_k`](dqre/subspaces.py#L92) (null)* | shared | 0.04 | +0.03 | +0.02 | 0.31 | floor |
```

The arrows earn their ink: they show the best `F2` row also has the worst `leak`, so `F2` is
buying recall with leakage. Bold falls on two different rows, saying it again without a sentence.
The null row is what makes 0.37 readable as a result rather than noise.

## Words around the table

Readers skim to the table and read nothing above it, so every part must stand alone. That is the
whole rule, and the slots below follow from it.

- **Title**: what this is, to someone who arrived cold. Name the thing being done. "Qwen3.5-4B
  sycophancy, -C" fails twice: it opens on the model, and it never says the page is about
  steering. "Can a steering vector make Qwen3.5-4B less sycophantic? (the -C direction)" costs
  eight more words and needs no context.
- **Subtitle**: what one row is. If a row is the best point of a sweep rather than a whole method,
  say so here or the ranking is misread.
- **Header**: short, because a header sets its column's width for every row below it.
- **Tooltip**: the per-column definitions. No width, no ink, and they cannot rot in a caption
  nobody updates. Markdown does these, contrary to what you would guess, using a reference-style
  link whose title is the definition and whose target is the code that computes the column:

      | [judge sel↑][sel] | [judge off↓][off][^1] |

      [sel]: scripts/score.py#L42 "on_axis minus 1.0 * off_axis"

  Use the reference form, never the inline one. An inline `[h](url "tip")` runs past 100
  characters and tabulate then pads every row in the column to match, which is the same damage
  pandoc does when it puts a title inside a header cell.
- **Footnote on a cell**: the traps. A tooltip is easy to never hover, so anything a reader must
  not miss goes here instead: a dose index that ranks nothing, a column that ignores sign.
- **Source note / caption**: the formula, provenance, and what the greyed rows are.

Read `annoy-less` before writing the prose ones, and keep them gentle rather than telegraphic.
They are sentences for a person, not a stack of `term: definition` fragments.

Say only what the table cannot say for itself. The arrow gives the direction, the heading gives
the group, and a column called `on_axis` under a heading about candour does not need a sentence
saying it measures movement toward candour. Ink is earned by the formula behind the headline, a
column that means something other than what its name suggests, and any trap that would make a
reader compare two cells that are not comparable.

Ink is NOT earned by defending your own design. "The weight is 1.0 rather than 0.1 because ..." is
a commit message; the reader wants to know it is 1.0. If the caption is longer than the table is
tall, you are writing documentation.

**A generated caption must not interpret.** In a finished paper the caption often carries a short
reading, with the longer argument in the body, and that is good writing because the numbers are
frozen. On a page a command regenerates, the numbers move and the sentence stays, so "vjp_delta
leads by a wide margin" survives the run where it stopped leading. Describe what the columns are
and what would mislead; leave what it means to the journal or the writeup, where it is dated and a
human owns it. The same applies to a figure caption on a generated page.

## What GFM actually supports

Measured against `gh api /markdown --mode gfm`, which is GitHub's own sanitizer, plus both VS Code
previews.

| want | verdict |
|---|---|
| tooltip | yes, reference-link title. `<abbr title>` is deleted, tag and all |
| footnote on a cell | GitHub and Markdown Preview Enhanced only. The built-in VS Code preview prints `[^1]` literally |
| merged header cell | no. `colspan` survives in a raw HTML table, but that costs you the pipe table |
| row shading | no. `style`, `class` and `bgcolor` are all stripped |
| small text | `<sub>` only. `<small>` and `<cite>` are stripped, text kept |
| collapsed detail | yes, `<details>`, and a markdown table nests inside it |
| colour | only `$\textcolor{}$` on github.com. Not worth the noise in the source |

Set the named parts apart with a heading, italic, and `<sub>`: title as `##` because that is the
only form that also gives an anchor and a TOC entry, subtitle italic because a reader who skips it
misranks the table, source note in `<sub>` because it is fine print, and open it with `Table:` so it reads as a caption
rather than as body text. Bold is not free for a title; it is already the best-cell mark.

Do not number tables. Rule 8 puts the newest group on top, so every run would renumber the ones
below it and any prose saying "as Table 3 shows" would quietly start pointing at the wrong run. The
heading gives each table an anchor, so refer to it by link. That also means the caption needs no
name: the title above it already says which table this is.

## Generating

The table is one part of a generated page. The page is the deliverable: a `just results` style
command with no GPU that reads cached artifacts and writes a dashboard for human review, holding
the master table, the master plot, one quoted demo per row, and links to the raw evidence. It is
also a goal to fill, so an empty cell is a visible task rather than a silent gap. It is
generator-owned, so hand-edits do not survive and nobody should try.

Markdown is the master format, not HTML. It diffs run to run, which answers "did the number move
after this fix", it greps, renders inline on GitHub, and
an agent recovering from a context reset can read it. HTML does none of those. So generate the
markdown page and treat any HTML as a companion view.

The structural fix for drift is to put the layout in a template file rather than in string
literals inside the generator, so a reviewer sees layout changes as layout. `string.Template` does
that with no dependency and is usually enough.

Quarto is the next step up when you also want inline python, one source emitting both markdown and
HTML, and cross-references, which is a writeup rather than a dashboard. `format: gfm` gives the
markdown; the python chunks need a jupyter kernel. Either way keep the computation in normal
scripts and let the document only display, so a broken document never costs you the numbers.
Marimo suits the interactive companion for browsing many samples side by side, but HTML is never
the master.

Compute once, render twice. A single dataframe is the source of truth; `tabulate` writes
`results.md` and `great_tables` writes `results.html`, and neither renderer computes anything. It
is only a fork if one renderer can produce a number the other cannot.

HTML is still worth adding, because two things markdown cannot do are what a wide results table
needs: spanner labels over grouped columns, and alternate-row shading.

Sizes, measured, because "HTML is huge" is only true of some HTML. `great_tables.write_raw_html`
emits plain HTML and CSS with no JavaScript: 19 KB for a 28-row, 6-column table. A marimo or
quarto self-contained export inlines its runtime and reaches megabytes, and that is the thing that
greps badly and burns an agent's context. Prefer raw great-tables HTML over a notebook export when
the page is a dashboard rather than a session.

**The HTML cannot be converted back into the markdown master.** Both routes were tried on a real
table with great-tables 0.23.0, and each drops a different half.

- `pandoc -f html -t gfm` does produce a pipe table, contradicting the obvious guess. It keeps the
  numbers, links and footnote markers, but bold-best and italic-controls vanish (they are inline
  CSS on the `td`, and markdown has nowhere to put CSS), spanners leak as raw `<span>`, the title
  ends up inside the first header cell and blows that column to hundreds of characters wide, and the
  minus sign becomes U+2212 so it stops matching `-` in grep.
- `GT.as_latex()` raises `NotImplementedError` if any `tab_footnote` is set, and once they are
  removed it warns that styles are unsupported and emits zero `\textbf` and zero `\textit`. What
  it does keep is the structure pandoc mangled: `\multicolumn` plus `\cmidrule` for spanners, and
  the title and subtitle as a real `\caption*`. The output is text and commits fine.

So the styling-as-predicate layer is HTML-only, which is exactly the layer that makes the table
readable at a glance. Generate markdown from the dataframe; never from the HTML.

polars to aggregate, tabulate to render:

print(tabulate(best, tablefmt="pipe", headers="keys", floatfmt="+.2f"))
```

The great-tables calls that carry the four principles worth borrowing:

```python
GT(display, rowname_col="method")                       # stub, distinct from the body
  .tab_header(title=..., subtitle=...)                  # named parts
  .tab_spanner(label="judge", columns=[...])            # grouped columns
  .fmt_number(columns=[...], decimals=2, force_sign=True)
  .tab_style(style.text(weight="bold"),                 # styling as a predicate, not a mark
             loc.body(columns="score", rows=pl.col("score") == df["score"].max()))

```

Print a SHOULD line after writing both: the two files must rank identically, because they read the
same dataframe, so a difference means a renderer is computing something it should not.

Write a prototype to a scratch path, never to `docs/`, until the layout is agreed. A draft table in
the results directory will be read as results.

### Two traps this pattern exposes

Both showed up the first time real numbers went through it, and neither is about rendering. That
is the argument for building the pipeline early: it makes the scoring rule visible.

**A coherence multiplier rewards collapse.** With `score = (on - w*off) * coh^2`, an arm whose
coherence fell to 0.02 is multiplied to about zero, which outranks a coherent method that honestly
scored negative. A destroyed run must sort last, not middle. Gate on coherence before scoring
instead of scaling by it.

**Best-of-sweep favours whoever was swept most.** Taking each method's best point is max
selection, so a method with 20 candidate points gets more draws than one with 3. Report the
candidate count per row, and size the bias off the null: if `random` only reaches +0.35 from 30
points, then two methods within a few tenths are tied rather than ranked.

A sparkline column can put back a curve that one-row-per-summary throws away. Use
[sparklines](https://github.com/deeplook/sparklines), never emit the blocks yourself, or you are
typing a picture of data you made up.

Tufte's argument for them is stronger than the obvious one, and it is about bias rather than
prettiness: a summary row shows only the current level or the recent change, which reinforces
recency, and the sparkline restores the history that the summary deleted. In his mutual-funds
example the numeric columns carry a couple of dozen values at five significant digits while the
sparklines beside them carry thousands at one or two. *Beautiful Evidence*, sparklines chapter,
searchable via the `tufte-viz` local corpus.

Then make it earn the column, which it often cannot in a small table. `start / min / end` is three
numbers, greppable and comparable across rows, and it answers most of what a loss curve is asked.
What it cannot show is what happened in between: a spike, a plateau, a late divergence. So reach
for a sparkline when the run is long enough that recency bias is real, or when mid-run shape is
itself the finding. Normalise each row to 0..1 first: the library emits ANSI inverse video for negative values, which
writes escape bytes into your markdown file and silently drops points. Normalising means it shows
shape and not level; say so or it lies.

When a table is the wrong shape for the answer, mermaid renders inline on GitHub and suits
anything with structure rather than magnitude.

## Borrowed from great-tables

[great-tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/user-guide/introduction.html) is HTML
first, so use it for an HTML view, not for the markdown page. Four of its ideas port anyway.

- Named parts. Title and subtitle above, stub (the index column) distinct from the body, source
  note below. "Caption" is vague; title above and source note below is the convention.
- Spanner labels group related columns. Markdown cannot span cells, so do it with a shared name
  prefix: `judge on_axis`, `judge off_axis`. Only where the bare header is ambiguous. `curve` and
  `pts` do not need a `dose` prefix, and the width it costs pushed the last column off screen.
- Cell footnotes. A `[^1]` marker on the exact column carries the definition out of the header
  without losing it, which is what makes short headers affordable.
- Styling is a predicate, not a manual mark. Bold-best and italic-controls should be a rule the
  generator applies, so they cannot go stale when the numbers change.

## What the literature adds

Sourced from wassname's local corpus, mostly secondhand because the primary texts are not
digitised. Paths are relative to `~/Documents/papers`.

**Is a table even right?** Tufte's threshold, quoted independently by three books, is that tables
beat a graph up to about 20 numbers, and also when the data is highly labelled or needs many
localised comparisons. Wainer sharpens it into a rule by count: up to 3 numbers write a sentence, 4 to 20
use a table, past 20 use a graph. A 13-row results table with 6 numeric columns is 78 numbers, so
the honest reading is that the table is the lookup and index, and the Pareto plot is the display.
Keep both; do not pretend the table is doing the graph's job.
(`books_bulk/.../Fleischer - Experimental Algorithmics (Springer, 2002).md:9230`,
`books_bulk/.../Galitz - Essential Guide to User Interface Design 3e [GUI] (Wiley, 2007).md:12467`)

**Ehrenberg's five rules**, as summarised by Seber
(`books_bulk/.../Seber - Multivariate Observations [mathematics] (Wiley, 2004).md:6909`):
round to two effective digits so numbers can be compared by eye; border the table with summary
statistics such as row and column averages; numbers are easier to compare down a column than
across a row; order rows and columns by size; and keep the numbers being compared close together.
Rule 1 is the one most often broken here: two decimals on a 0..5 judge scale whose interval is
+/-1.5 wide is a third significant digit of noise. Rule 2 is what the floor and baseline rows are
already doing, so treat them as the anchor they are and keep them adjacent to the candidates
rather than exiled to the bottom.

**Sample size caps your digits.** Peat's rule is that under 50 observations each one is worth more
than 2%, so whole percentages only, and under 20 each is worth 5% and whole numbers are "more
honest". A score averaged over 20 items does not get two decimals.
(`books_bulk/.../Scientific Writing - Easy When You Know How - J Peat (BMJ 2002).md:4118`)

**Alphabetical order is a wasted axis.** Myatt: it may serve as an index but "almost always
reveals nothing more"; order by the most important variable instead.
(`books_bulk/.../Myatt - Making Sense of Data II - Practical Guide to Data Visualization (Wiley, 2009).md:1680`)

**Rules and separators.** Journal convention is few horizontal rules and no vertical rules; fancy
borders and grids distract (Peat, `:4144`). Tullis measured it on screen: alternate-row shading
beat both full grids and horizontal separators for search speed and accuracy, because borders
interfere with scanning, and where shading is unavailable or the table passes seven rows, add
white space after every fifth row (Galitz, `:10339`). Markdown can do neither, which is one honest
reason to also emit an HTML view once a table is long.

**A conflict worth knowing about.** Peat argues the title plus detailed row and column descriptors
should carry the essential information and that footnotes "should be avoided as far as possible"
(`:4217`). That cuts against using a footnote for a trap. Both can be right: a footnote is wrong
for something the reader needs in order to read the table at all, and right for a caveat that only
bites if they try a comparison the table does not support. If you can fit it in the header, do.

## Related skills

`tufte-viz` for the parent principles. Three transfer to tables directly: the eraser test (erase a
column, is anything lost that is not already said elsewhere? this is how you catch `off_axis mean`
plus `off_axis max`), lie factor (significant figures beyond your precision, and sorting
incomparable groups into one ranking), and small multiples (which is exactly rule 8, so the group
tables must share a column order). It also suggests an in-table sparkline, `` `▁▂▄▆█▅▂` ``, which
puts back the dose curve that one-row-per-method throws away.

`annoy-less` for the caption prose. Note the deliberate exception: its "no bold invasion" rule
does not apply inside the table, where bold is the best-cell encoding, but it does apply to the
caption around it.

## Why it drifts

Appending a column is the cheapest way to surface a new number and nobody ever deletes one, so the
headline gets pushed right one defensible commit at a time. A template file beside the generator
has no force, because whoever edits the generator reads the generator. Put the rule as a
comment at the line where the header list is defined. A substring-presence check will not save
you: it cannot see column order, so it passes while the shape rots.

## Self-check

- Index in column 1, headline in column 2, its inputs next?
- Sorted by the headline, best first?
- Arrow on every header, and every header short?
- Best cell bold, controls and baselines italic, floors present?
- One table per comparable group, newest on top, same columns?
- Erase each column: is anything lost? If not, cut it.
- Do both renderers read one dataframe, and does neither compute?
- Does the run print the candidate count per row?
- Does a collapsed row sort last rather than near zero?
- Is the prototype outside `docs/`?
- Do the markdown and the HTML rank identically?

# Markdown results tables

## The rule

It is a publication table. Ink and leftmost above-the-fold space are the two scarce resources, so
spend both only on what answers the reader's question. Order left to right by decreasing
importance and top to bottom by rank. Make typography carry meaning rather than decoration.

Everything below follows from that. Remember the rule and you will get most of it right.

## Consequences

1. Column 1 is the index, linked to its source. Then short metadata if rows need it. Then the
   headline score. Nothing else goes left of the headline.
2. The headline's own inputs follow it, in formula order, so the arithmetic is checkable in place.
3. Sort by the headline, best first. The answer is the first line read.
4. A unicode arrow on every header, glued to the last word: `sel↑`, `off↓`, `drift→0`. A space
   there lets the header wrap and strand the arrow on its own line, which was visible in both VS
   Code previews.
5. Bold the best cell per column, unless the best value covers over half the column. Seven bold
   `1.00`s out of thirteen rows say nothing. Italicise controls and baselines.
6. Always carry the floors and the bar. A number with nothing to beat means nothing.
7. Short headers. A header sets its column's width for every row below it. Definitions live in
   the caption.
8. One table per comparable group, most recent on top, identical columns in each.
9. Last column `notes` is free real estate: links to the evidence, and `<!-- CLAUDE: ... -->`
   comments that are invisible rendered but readable by the next agent.

## Example, before and after

wassname's, from dqre. Already good: name links to `file#line` so provenance costs no width, then
metadata, then the headline `F2`, then the components `F2` is made of, sorted by headline.

```markdown
| subspace | form | F2 | recall: en at L27 | leak: fr at L32 | precision |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [`en_minus_null`](dqre/subspaces.py#L176) | shared | 0.37 | 0.33 | +0.16 | 0.68 |
| [`unembed_top`](dqre/subspaces.py#L119) | shared | 0.21 | 0.17 | +0.07 | 0.71 |
| [`en_minus_null_perp_all`](dqre/subspaces.py#L180) | shared | 0.19 | 0.16 | +0.05 | 0.76 |
```

Missing arrows, bold-best, a floor, and the headers are long. Fixed:

```markdown
| subspace | form | F2 ↑ | recall en@L27 ↑ | leak fr@L32 ↓ | precision ↑ | notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| [`en_minus_null`](dqre/subspaces.py#L176) | shared | **0.37** | **+0.33** | +0.16 | 0.68 | [res](out/a.jsonl) |
| [`unembed_top`](dqre/subspaces.py#L119) | shared | 0.21 | +0.17 | +0.07 | 0.71 | [res](out/b.jsonl) |
| [`en_minus_null_perp_all`](dqre/subspaces.py#L180) | shared | 0.19 | +0.16 | **+0.05** | **0.76** | [res](out/c.jsonl) |
| *[`random_rank_k`](dqre/subspaces.py#L92) (null)* | shared | 0.04 | +0.03 | +0.02 | 0.31 | floor |
```

The arrows earn their ink: they show the best `F2` row also has the worst `leak`, so `F2` is
buying recall with leakage. Bold falls on two different rows, saying it again without a sentence.
The null row is what makes 0.37 readable as a result rather than noise.

## Words around the table

Readers skim to the table and read nothing above it, so every part must stand alone. That is the
whole rule, and the slots below follow from it.

- **Title**: what this is, to someone who arrived cold. Name the thing being done. "Qwen3.5-4B
  sycophancy, -C" fails twice: it opens on the model, and it never says the page is about
  steering. "Can a steering vector make Qwen3.5-4B less sycophantic? (the -C direction)" costs
  eight more words and needs no context.
- **Subtitle**: what one row is. If a row is the best point of a sweep rather than a whole method,
  say so here or the ranking is misread.
- **Header**: short, because a header sets its column's width for every row below it.
- **Tooltip**: the per-column definitions. No width, no ink, and they cannot rot in a caption
  nobody updates. Markdown does these, contrary to what you would guess, using a reference-style
  link whose title is the definition and whose target is the code that computes the column:

      | [judge sel↑][sel] | [judge off↓][off][^1] |

      [sel]: scripts/score.py#L42 "on_axis minus 1.0 * off_axis"

  Use the reference form, never the inline one. An inline `[h](url "tip")` runs past 100
  characters and tabulate then pads every row in the column to match, which is the same damage
  pandoc does when it puts a title inside a header cell.
- **Footnote on a cell**: the traps. A tooltip is easy to never hover, so anything a reader must
  not miss goes here instead: a dose index that ranks nothing, a column that ignores sign.
- **Source note / caption**: the formula, provenance, and what the greyed rows are.

Read `annoy-less` before writing the prose ones, and keep them gentle rather than telegraphic.
They are sentences for a person, not a stack of `term: definition` fragments.

Say only what the table cannot say for itself. The arrow gives the direction, the heading gives
the group, and a column called `on_axis` under a heading about candour does not need a sentence
saying it measures movement toward candour. Ink is earned by the formula behind the headline, a
column that means something other than what its name suggests, and any trap that would make a
reader compare two cells that are not comparable.

Ink is NOT earned by defending your own design. "The weight is 1.0 rather than 0.1 because ..." is
a commit message; the reader wants to know it is 1.0. If the caption is longer than the table is
tall, you are writing documentation.

**A generated caption must not interpret.** In a finished paper the caption often carries a short
reading, with the longer argument in the body, and that is good writing because the numbers are
frozen. On a page a command regenerates, the numbers move and the sentence stays, so "vjp_delta
leads by a wide margin" survives the run where it stopped leading. Describe what the columns are
and what would mislead; leave what it means to the journal or the writeup, where it is dated and a
human owns it. The same applies to a figure caption on a generated page.

## What GFM actually supports

Measured against `gh api /markdown --mode gfm`, which is GitHub's own sanitizer, plus both VS Code
previews.

| want | verdict |
|---|---|
| tooltip | yes, reference-link title. `<abbr title>` is deleted, tag and all |
| footnote on a cell | GitHub and Markdown Preview Enhanced only. The built-in VS Code preview prints `[^1]` literally |
| merged header cell | no. `colspan` survives in a raw HTML table, but that costs you the pipe table |
| row shading | no. `style`, `class` and `bgcolor` are all stripped |
| small text | `<sub>` only. `<small>` and `<cite>` are stripped, text kept |
| collapsed detail | yes, `<details>`, and a markdown table nests inside it |
| colour | only `$\textcolor{}$` on github.com. Not worth the noise in the source |

Set the named parts apart with a heading, italic, and `<sub>`: title as `##` because that is the
only form that also gives an anchor and a TOC entry, subtitle italic because a reader who skips it
misranks the table, source note in `<sub>` because it is fine print, and open it with `Table:` so it reads as a caption
rather than as body text. Bold is not free for a title; it is already the best-cell mark.

Do not number tables. Rule 8 puts the newest group on top, so every run would renumber the ones
below it and any prose saying "as Table 3 shows" would quietly start pointing at the wrong run. The
heading gives each table an anchor, so refer to it by link. That also means the caption needs no
name: the title above it already says which table this is.

## Generating

The table is one part of a generated page. The page is the deliverable: a `just results` style
command with no GPU that reads cached artifacts and writes a dashboard for human review, holding
the master table, the master plot, one quoted demo per row, and links to the raw evidence. It is
also a goal to fill, so an empty cell is a visible task rather than a silent gap. It is
generator-owned, so hand-edits do not survive and nobody should try.

Markdown is the master format, not HTML. It diffs run to run, which answers "did the number move
after this fix", it greps, renders inline on GitHub, and
an agent recovering from a context reset can read it. HTML does none of those. So generate the
markdown page and treat any HTML as a companion view.

The structural fix for drift is to put the layout in a template file rather than in string
literals inside the generator, so a reviewer sees layout changes as layout. `string.Template` does
that with no dependency and is usually enough.

Quarto is the next step up when you also want inline python, one source emitting both markdown and
HTML, and cross-references, which is a writeup rather than a dashboard. `format: gfm` gives the
markdown; the python chunks need a jupyter kernel. Either way keep the computation in normal
scripts and let the document only display, so a broken document never costs you the numbers.
Marimo suits the interactive companion for browsing many samples side by side, but HTML is never
the master.

Compute once, render twice. A single dataframe is the source of truth; `tabulate` writes
`results.md` and `great_tables` writes `results.html`, and neither renderer computes anything. It
is only a fork if one renderer can produce a number the other cannot.

HTML is still worth adding, because two things markdown cannot do are what a wide results table
needs: spanner labels over grouped columns, and alternate-row shading.

Sizes, measured, because "HTML is huge" is only true of some HTML. `great_tables.write_raw_html`
emits plain HTML and CSS with no JavaScript: 19 KB for a 28-row, 6-column table. A marimo or
quarto self-contained export inlines its runtime and reaches megabytes, and that is the thing that
greps badly and burns an agent's context. Prefer raw great-tables HTML over a notebook export when
the page is a dashboard rather than a session.

**The HTML cannot be converted back into the markdown master.** Both routes were tried on a real
table with great-tables 0.23.0, and each drops a different half.

- `pandoc -f html -t gfm` does produce a pipe table, contradicting the obvious guess. It keeps the
  numbers, links and footnote markers, but bold-best and italic-controls vanish (they are inline
  CSS on the `td`, and markdown has nowhere to put CSS), spanners leak as raw `<span>`, the title
  ends up inside the first header cell and blows that column to hundreds of characters wide, and the
  minus sign becomes U+2212 so it stops matching `-` in grep.
- `GT.as_latex()` raises `NotImplementedError` if any `tab_footnote` is set, and once they are
  removed it warns that styles are unsupported and emits zero `\textbf` and zero `\textit`. What
  it does keep is the structure pandoc mangled: `\multicolumn` plus `\cmidrule` for spanners, and
  the title and subtitle as a real `\caption*`. The output is text and commits fine.

So the styling-as-predicate layer is HTML-only, which is exactly the layer that makes the table
readable at a glance. Generate markdown from the dataframe; never from the HTML.

polars to aggregate, tabulate to render:

```python
best = (df.filter(pl.col("usable"))
          .sort("selectivity", descending=True)
          .group_by("method").first())     # one row per method: the best point of its sweep
print(tabulate(best, tablefmt="pipe", headers="keys", floatfmt="+.2f"))
```

`disable_numparse=True` keeps pre-formatted cells (bold, links, arrows) intact. Keep the header
list as one ordered literal so a reviewer sees column order change in the diff.

```python
def best_points(damage_weight: float) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """One row per method: the point of its sweep with the highest headline score."""

def to_markdown(df, w) -> str:   # tabulate, disable_numparse=True keeps bold/links/arrows intact
def to_html(df, w) -> GT:        # great_tables over the SAME df
```

The great-tables calls that carry the four principles worth borrowing:

```python
GT(display, rowname_col="method")                       # stub, distinct from the body
  .tab_header(title=..., subtitle=...)                  # named parts
  .tab_spanner(label="judge", columns=[...])            # grouped columns
  .fmt_number(columns=[...], decimals=2, force_sign=True)
  .tab_style(style.text(weight="bold"),                 # styling as a predicate, not a mark
             loc.body(columns="score", rows=pl.col("score") == df["score"].max()))
  .tab_source_note(...)                                 # provenance below the table
```

Print a SHOULD line after writing both: the two files must rank identically, because they read the
same dataframe, so a difference means a renderer is computing something it should not.

Write a prototype to a scratch path, never to `docs/`, until the layout is agreed. A draft table in
the results directory will be read as results.

### Two traps this pattern exposes

Both showed up the first time real numbers went through it, and neither is about rendering. That
is the argument for building the pipeline early: it makes the scoring rule visible.

**A coherence multiplier rewards collapse.** With `score = (on - w*off) * coh^2`, an arm whose
coherence fell to 0.02 is multiplied to about zero, which outranks a coherent method that honestly
scored negative. A destroyed run must sort last, not middle. Gate on coherence before scoring
instead of scaling by it.

**Best-of-sweep favours whoever was swept most.** Taking each method's best point is max
selection, so a method with 20 candidate points gets more draws than one with 3. Report the
candidate count per row, and size the bias off the null: if `random` only reaches +0.35 from 30
points, then two methods within a few tenths are tied rather than ranked.

A sparkline column can put back a curve that one-row-per-summary throws away. Use
[sparklines](https://github.com/deeplook/sparklines), never emit the blocks yourself, or you are
typing a picture of data you made up.

Tufte's argument for them is stronger than the obvious one, and it is about bias rather than
prettiness: a summary row shows only the current level or the recent change, which reinforces
recency, and the sparkline restores the history that the summary deleted. In his mutual-funds
example the numeric columns carry a couple of dozen values at five significant digits while the
sparklines beside them carry thousands at one or two. *Beautiful Evidence*, sparklines chapter,
searchable via the `tufte-viz` local corpus.

Then make it earn the column, which it often cannot in a small table. `start / min / end` is three
numbers, greppable and comparable across rows, and it answers most of what a loss curve is asked.
What it cannot show is what happened in between: a spike, a plateau, a late divergence. So reach
for a sparkline when the run is long enough that recency bias is real, or when mid-run shape is
itself the finding. Normalise each row to 0..1 first: the library emits ANSI inverse video for negative values, which
writes escape bytes into your markdown file and silently drops points. Normalising means it shows
shape and not level; say so or it lies.

When a table is the wrong shape for the answer, mermaid renders inline on GitHub and suits
anything with structure rather than magnitude.

## Borrowed from great-tables

[great-tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/user-guide/introduction.html) is HTML
first, so use it for an HTML view, not for the markdown page. Four of its ideas port anyway.

- Named parts. Title and subtitle above, stub (the index column) distinct from the body, source
  note below. "Caption" is vague; title above and source note below is the convention.
- Spanner labels group related columns. Markdown cannot span cells, so do it with a shared name
  prefix: `judge on_axis`, `judge off_axis`. Only where the bare header is ambiguous. `curve` and
  `pts` do not need a `dose` prefix, and the width it costs pushed the last column off screen.
- Cell footnotes. A `[^1]` marker on the exact column carries the definition out of the header
  without losing it, which is what makes short headers affordable.
- Styling is a predicate, not a manual mark. Bold-best and italic-controls should be a rule the
  generator applies, so they cannot go stale when the numbers change.

## What the literature adds

Sourced from wassname's local corpus, mostly secondhand because the primary texts are not
digitised. Paths are relative to `~/Documents/papers`.

**Is a table even right?** Tufte's threshold, quoted independently by three books, is that tables
beat a graph up to about 20 numbers, and also when the data is highly labelled or needs many
localised comparisons. Wainer sharpens it into a rule by count: up to 3 numbers write a sentence, 4 to 20
use a table, past 20 use a graph. A 13-row results table with 6 numeric columns is 78 numbers, so
the honest reading is that the table is the lookup and index, and the Pareto plot is the display.
Keep both; do not pretend the table is doing the graph's job.
(`books_bulk/.../Fleischer - Experimental Algorithmics (Springer, 2002).md:9230`,
`books_bulk/.../Galitz - Essential Guide to User Interface Design 3e [GUI] (Wiley, 2007).md:12467`)

**Ehrenberg's five rules**, as summarised by Seber
(`books_bulk/.../Seber - Multivariate Observations [mathematics] (Wiley, 2004).md:6909`):
round to two effective digits so numbers can be compared by eye; border the table with summary
statistics such as row and column averages; numbers are easier to compare down a column than
across a row; order rows and columns by size; and keep the numbers being compared close together.
Rule 1 is the one most often broken here: two decimals on a 0..5 judge scale whose interval is
+/-1.5 wide is a third significant digit of noise. Rule 2 is what the floor and baseline rows are
already doing, so treat them as the anchor they are and keep them adjacent to the candidates
rather than exiled to the bottom.

**Sample size caps your digits.** Peat's rule is that under 50 observations each one is worth more
than 2%, so whole percentages only, and under 20 each is worth 5% and whole numbers are "more
honest". A score averaged over 20 items does not get two decimals.
(`books_bulk/.../Scientific Writing - Easy When You Know How - J Peat (BMJ 2002).md:4118`)

**Alphabetical order is a wasted axis.** Myatt: it may serve as an index but "almost always
reveals nothing more"; order by the most important variable instead.
(`books_bulk/.../Myatt - Making Sense of Data II - Practical Guide to Data Visualization (Wiley, 2009).md:1680`)

**Rules and separators.** Journal convention is few horizontal rules and no vertical rules; fancy
borders and grids distract (Peat, `:4144`). Tullis measured it on screen: alternate-row shading
beat both full grids and horizontal separators for search speed and accuracy, because borders
interfere with scanning, and where shading is unavailable or the table passes seven rows, add
white space after every fifth row (Galitz, `:10339`). Markdown can do neither, which is one honest
reason to also emit an HTML view once a table is long.

**A conflict worth knowing about.** Peat argues the title plus detailed row and column descriptors
should carry the essential information and that footnotes "should be avoided as far as possible"
(`:4217`). That cuts against using a footnote for a trap. Both can be right: a footnote is wrong
for something the reader needs in order to read the table at all, and right for a caveat that only
bites if they try a comparison the table does not support. If you can fit it in the header, do.

## Related skills

`tufte-viz` for the parent principles. Three transfer to tables directly: the eraser test (erase a
column, is anything lost that is not already said elsewhere? this is how you catch `off_axis mean`
plus `off_axis max`), lie factor (significant figures beyond your precision, and sorting
incomparable groups into one ranking), and small multiples (which is exactly rule 8, so the group
tables must share a column order). It also suggests an in-table sparkline, `` `▁▂▄▆█▅▂` ``, which
puts back the dose curve that one-row-per-method throws away.

`annoy-less` for the caption prose. Note the deliberate exception: its "no bold invasion" rule
does not apply inside the table, where bold is the best-cell encoding, but it does apply to the
caption around it.

## Why it drifts

Appending a column is the cheapest way to surface a new number and nobody ever deletes one, so the
headline gets pushed right one defensible commit at a time. A template file beside the generator
has no force, because whoever edits the generator reads the generator. Put the rule as a
comment at the line where the header list is defined. A substring-presence check will not save
you: it cannot see column order, so it passes while the shape rots.

## Self-check

- Index in column 1, headline in column 2, its inputs next?
- Sorted by the headline, best first?
- Arrow on every header, and every header short?
- Best cell bold, controls and baselines italic, floors present?
- One table per comparable group, newest on top, same columns?
- Erase each column: is anything lost? If not, cut it.
- Do both renderers read one dataframe, and does neither compute?
- Does the run print the candidate count per row?
- Does a collapsed row sort last rather than near zero?
- Is the prototype outside `docs/`?
- Do the markdown and the HTML rank identically?
